draft.title: Stationary points
card: A stationary point is where the gradient of the curve is zero. To find one, solve f'(x) = 0 and then put each x value into f(x) to get the y value.
To find its type, check the sign of f'(x) just before and just after the point. Put the results in a table of gradients.
the gradient goes from positive to zero to negative. Minimum: it goes from negative to zero to positive.

the gradient has the same sign on both sides. Example: f(x) = x³ − 3x². Then f'(x) = 3x² − 6x = 3x(x − 2), so x = 0 or 2. At x = −1, f' = 9 (positive). At x = 1, f' = −3 (negative). At x = 3, f' = 9 (positive). So x = 0 is a maximum and x = 2 is a minimum.
draft.remember: Solve f'(x) = 0, then test the gradient on each side to name the type.

a.q: A curve has f'(x) = 0 at x = 4. The gradient is negative just before x = 4 and positive just after. What type of stationary point is it?
a.why: The gradient goes from negative to zero to positive, so the curve falls and then rises. That is a minimum. It is not a maximum, because a maximum has the gradient going from positive to negative.
a.clue: Picture the curve going down and then up.

b.q: For f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x, what is the stationary point at x = 3?
opts: A horizontal point of inflection at (3, 0)
b.why: f'(x) = 3x² − 12x + 9 = 3(x − 1)(x − 3), so f'(x) = 0 at x = 3. At x = 2, f' = −3. At x = 4, f' = 9. The gradient goes from negative to positive, so it is a minimum. f(3) = 27 − 54 + 27 = 0, so the point is (3, 0). The point (3, 9) comes from a wrong y value.
b.clue: Test the gradient at x = 2 and x = 4, then find f(3).

problems.detail: The worked example (f(x) = x³ − 3x², giving a maximum and a minimum) sits in the 'Horizontal inflection' bullet, so it seems to illustrate a horizontal inflection when it shows none. It should go in its own bullet or with the maximum/minimum bullet.

proposal.title: Stationary points
card: A stationary point is where the gradient of the curve is zero. To find one, solve f'(x) = 0, then put each x value into f(x) to get the y value.

To find its type, check the sign of f'(x) just before and just after the point, and record it in a table of gradients. Positive to zero to negative is a maximum. Negative to zero to positive is a minimum.
If the gradient has the same sign on both sides, such as positive, zero, positive, the point is a horizontal point of inflection.
Example: f(x) = x³ − 3x², so f'(x) = 3x² − 6x = 3x(x − 2) = 0 at x = 0 or 2. At x = −1, 1 and 3, f' is 9, −3 and 9, so (0, 0) is a maximum and (2, −4) is a minimum.
proposal.remember: Solve f'(x) = 0, then test the gradient on each side to name the type.

b.why: f'(x) = 3x² − 12x + 9 = 3(x − 1)(x − 3), so f'(x) = 0 at x = 3. At x = 2, f' = −3, and at x = 4, f' = 9, so the gradient goes from negative to positive: a minimum. f(3) = 27 − 54 + 27 = 0, so the point is (3, 0), not (3, 9), which mixes up a gradient value with the y value.
